opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most underappreciated aspects of the agents conversation. There's a tendency to treat it purely as a capability problem — once the models get good enough, agents will just work. But I think a lot of the real friction is economic and political, not technical.

On the economic side, look at what many of the most hyped agent use cases actually require. If you want an agent to book flights or shop for you, it has to interact with websites and platforms whose business models depend on a human being there — seeing ads, getting upsold, being steered toward certain options. Those companies don't necessarily want an agent showing up, comparison shopping ruthlessly, and skipping all of that. So you can expect a lot of them to resist: blocking agents, changing their terms of service, or building their own walled-garden agents that serve their interests rather than the user's. We've seen versions of this before with scraping and with APIs that got locked down once platforms realized third parties were capturing value.

Then there's the question of who the agent actually works for. If an agent is provided by a company that also earns money from advertisers or partners, there's an obvious conflict of interest. With a search engine, you can at least see the results and judge for yourself. With an agent that just acts, that steering becomes much harder to detect. So trust becomes a central economic issue, not a side concern.

On the political and policy side, there are hard questions about liability and accountability. When an agent makes a mistake — buys the wrong thing, sends the wrong email, agrees to something on your behalf — who's responsible? The user, the developer, the platform? Our legal frameworks aren't really set up for software that takes consequential actions semi-autonomously. And until those questions have reasonable answers, a lot of businesses and individuals will be cautious about delegating anything that really matters.

So my view is that agent adoption will be slower and messier than the most optimistic predictions, and that's not mainly because the models aren't smart enough. It's because deploying them means renegotiating relationships between users, platforms, and businesses, and that kind of change has historically taken years or decades, not months. Capability is necessary, but it's far from sufficient.

r001.rationale: The response discusses platforms resisting agents and third parties capturing value, but it does not identify equitable distribution of the economic value created by agents as a problem that must be resolved.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think when people talk about the challenges of agents, they mostly talk about the technical ones — reliability, the fact that errors compound over long sequences of steps, that kind of thing. And those are real. But I've come to think the economic and political challenges might actually be the harder ones, and they get much less attention.

Let me start with the economic side. The vision of agents that gets sold is something like: you tell the agent to book you a trip, and it goes out, compares flights, picks a hotel, makes the reservations, done. But think about what that actually requires. It requires airlines and hotels and booking platforms to let an agent act on your behalf. And why would they? Their whole business model is built around having your attention — showing you the upsell, the ads, the "customers also bought." An agent that just gets in, does the task, and gets out is, from their perspective, a bad customer. So you get this situation where the people who own the interfaces have every incentive to block agents, or to degrade the experience for them, or to cut deals only with certain agent providers. We're already seeing that with sites blocking crawlers, and I think it's going to intensify.

And that leads to the second economic issue, which is who the agent actually works for. If the agent is built by a company that also has commercial relationships with the merchants, there's a real question about whose interests it's optimizing. We've seen this movie before with search engines and with app stores. The intermediary starts out as a neutral helper and gradually becomes a tollbooth. So I don't think "will the agent work" is the right question — it's "will the agent work for me."

Then there's the political side, and I mean that broadly — questions of power, accountability, and governance. One piece is liability. When an agent makes a mistake, and it will, who's responsible? The developer? The user who deployed it? The company whose API it called? Right now the answer is basically nobody has figured that out, and that uncertainty itself slows adoption. Businesses don't want to deploy something where they can't model the downside.

Another piece is that agents concentrate capabilities. The things agents are good at — automating workflows, generating content at scale, interacting with lots of systems at once — those benefit whoever can deploy them most widely. That tends to be the already-powerful actors. So I worry a bit less about the sci-fi scenarios and more about the fairly mundane scenario where agents just become another force amplifying existing inequalities, unless we're deliberate about it.

And then there's the governance question of how you even regulate this. A lot of the policy conversation has been about models — how big is the model, what are its capabilities. But agents are mostly about what you do with the model, the scaffolding around it, the permissions you give it. That's much harder to regulate at the model level, and I think the policy world is still catching up to that shift.

So my overall view is that we'll solve a lot of the technical problems, probably faster than people expect. But the hard part is that agents don't exist in a vacuum — they exist in an economy and a society that has to decide whether to accommodate them and on whose terms. And that's a negotiation, not an engineering problem.

r001.rationale: The response worries that agents may amplify existing inequalities, but it does not clearly identify how the economic value created by agents is distributed as a problem that must be resolved.

astra-6.text:
I think the technical question—can we build an agent that performs a task reliably—is only part of the story. The economic question is: whose interests does that agent serve? You might think of it as your assistant, but if a company provides it, and that company makes money from advertising or commissions, there’s a potential conflict between what’s best for you and what’s profitable for the provider.

Take an agent that shops on your behalf. Comparing products is a technical problem. But whether retailers allow it access, whether it can complete purchases, and whether its recommendations are influenced by commercial relationships are questions about incentives and bargaining power. Even a very capable agent has to operate within that environment.

And that becomes a political question when we ask who controls the infrastructure. If a few companies mediate a large share of our interactions with businesses and public services, they acquire considerable power over which options we see and which actions we can take. What ability do users have to switch providers? Who is accountable when something goes wrong?

So I wouldn’t assume that improving capabilities automatically gets us useful, trustworthy agents. We also need business models and institutions that make it possible for those agents to act in our interests.

r001.rationale: The response discusses conflicts between users’ interests and providers’ profits, but does not identify equitable distribution of the economic value created by AI agents as a problem to resolve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it helps to separate what an agent can do in a demo from what it takes to make it useful in the economy. A demo might show an agent booking a trip or completing a programming task. But in practice, you care about how often it fails, how much supervision it needs, and whether the cost of catching and correcting its mistakes wipes out the time you saved. Those are economic questions as much as technical ones.

And then the agent has to interact with other people’s systems. If my agent goes to a website on my behalf, does that website want to cooperate? Its business model might depend on showing me ads or influencing my choices. So even if we solve the technical problem of having software navigate the web, we haven’t solved the incentive problem. The other side can change the interface, restrict access, or charge for it.

The political question is who gets to set the terms. Who can authorize an agent to act? Who is responsible when it makes a consequential mistake? And if a small number of companies control the agents through which we access services, they gain a lot of power over both consumers and businesses.

So I don’t see this as simply a matter of making models smarter and then waiting for agents to take over tasks. Making them work requires institutions, accountability, and agreements among parties whose interests often conflict. That part is likely to be much slower and messier than the demos suggest.

r001.rationale: The response discusses agents’ costs, business incentives, and concentrated power, but does not identify equitable distribution of the economic value created by agents as a problem to resolve.
